entry.title: 1. Linear Algebra Essentials
entry.content:
Linear algebra is the language of data. Every dataset is a matrix, every feature is a vector, and every model transformation is a linear map.

Vectors and Inner Products

A vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ represents a point or direction in $n$-dimensional space. The inner product measures similarity:

\[\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle = \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{y} = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i\]

The $\ell_2$ norm $|\mathbf{x}| = \sqrt{\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{x}}$ measures magnitude. Two vectors are orthogonal if $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle = 0$.

Matrices as Linear Maps

A matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ defines a linear transformation $f(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$. Key properties:

  • Rank: $\text{rank}(A)$ = dimension of the column space = number of linearly independent columns
  • Determinant: $\det(A) \neq 0 \Leftrightarrow A$ is invertible (for square matrices)
  • Trace: $\text{tr}(A) = \sum_i A_{ii}$, invariant under cyclic permutations: $\text{tr}(ABC) = \text{tr}(CAB)$

Eigendecomposition

For a square matrix $A$, an eigenvector $\mathbf{v}$ satisfies $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v}$, where $\lambda$ is the corresponding eigenvalue.

If $A$ is symmetric ($A = A^\top$), it admits a spectral decomposition:

\[A = Q \Lambda Q^\top\]

where $Q$ is orthogonal ($Q^\top Q = I$) and $\Lambda = \text{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)$.

This is the foundation of PCA: projecting data onto the top eigenvectors of the covariance matrix.

Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)

Any matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ can be decomposed as:

\[A = U \Sigma V^\top\]

where $U \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}$, $V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ are orthogonal, and $\Sigma$ contains the singular values $\sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \cdots \geq 0$.

SVD provides the best rank-$k$ approximation (Eckart–Young theorem):

\[A_k = \sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{v}_i^\top = \arg\min_{\text{rank}(B)=k} \|A - B\|_F\]

Positive Definite Matrices

A symmetric matrix $A$ is positive definite ($A \succ 0$) if $\mathbf{x}^\top A \mathbf{x} > 0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \neq 0$, equivalently, all eigenvalues are positive.

Positive definiteness ensures:

  • Convexity of $f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^\top A \mathbf{x}$ — critical for optimization
  • Unique solutions to $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$
  • A valid covariance matrix in probability

Reference

G. Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra, 6th ed. Wellesley-Cambridge Press, 2023.
entry.summary: Linear algebra is the language of data — covering vectors, matrices, eigendecomposition, SVD, and positive definite matrices essential for machine learning.

entry.title: 2. Calculus for Optimization
entry.content:
Most of machine learning reduces to optimization — minimizing a loss function. Calculus gives us the tools to find and characterize these minima.

Partial Derivatives and the Gradient

For a scalar function $f: \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}$, the gradient collects all partial derivatives:

\[ abla f(\mathbf{x}) = egin{bmatrix} rac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} \ \vdots \ rac{\partial f}{\partial x_n} \end{bmatrix}\]

The gradient points in the direction of steepest ascent. Moving opposite to the gradient decreases $f$ — this is the basis of gradient descent.

Chain Rule

For composed functions $f = g \circ h$, the chain rule is:

\[ rac{\partial f}{\partial x} = rac{\partial g}{\partial h} \cdot rac{\partial h}{\partial x}\]

For vector-valued functions, this generalizes to Jacobian multiplication, which is exactly what backpropagation computes through the computational graph of a neural network.

The Hessian

The Hessian $H \in \mathbb{R}^{n imes n}$ is the matrix of second-order partial derivatives:

\[H_{ij} = rac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}\]

The Hessian characterizes local curvature:

  • $H \succ 0$ (positive definite) at a critical point → local minimum
  • $H \prec 0$ → local maximum
  • $H$ indefinite → saddle point

Taylor Expansion

The second-order Taylor expansion around $\mathbf{x}_0$:

\[f(\mathbf{x}) \approx f(\mathbf{x}_0) + abla f(\mathbf{x}_0)^ op (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0) + rac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0)^ op H(\mathbf{x}_0) (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0)\]

This quadratic approximation motivates Newton’s method: the update $\Delta \mathbf{x} = -H^{-1} abla f$ jumps directly to the minimum of the local quadratic model.

Matrix Calculus Identities

Useful identities that appear frequently in ML derivations:

Expression Derivative
$\mathbf{a}^ op \mathbf{x}$ $\mathbf{a}$
$\mathbf{x}^ op A \mathbf{x}$ $(A + A^ op)\mathbf{x}$
$|A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}|^2$ $2A^ op(A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b})$
$ ext{tr}(A^ op B)$ $B$
$\log \det(A)$ $A^{- op}$

Reference

S. Boyd, L. Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization. Cambridge University Press, 2004, Ch. 2–3.
entry.summary: Calculus provides the tools for finding and characterizing minima of loss functions, covering gradients, the chain rule, Hessians, and Taylor expansions.

entry.title: 3. Probability Fundamentals
entry.content:
Probability theory is the framework for reasoning under uncertainty. Every ML model is, at its core, a probabilistic statement about data.

Probability Space

A probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$ consists of:

  • Sample space $\Omega$: set of all possible outcomes
  • Event algebra $\mathcal{F}$: collection of measurable subsets of $\Omega$
  • Probability measure $P: \mathcal{F} \to [0, 1]$ satisfying $P(\Omega) = 1$ and countable additivity

Conditional Probability and Independence

Conditional probability: given that $B$ occurred,

\[P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}, \quad P(B) > 0\]

Events $A$ and $B$ are independent if $P(A \cap B) = P(A) P(B)$.

Bayes’ Rule

The cornerstone of probabilistic inference:

\[P(\theta \mid D) = \frac{P(D \mid \theta) \, P(\theta)}{P(D)}\]
Term Name Role
$P(\theta \mid D)$ Posterior What we want to know
$P(D \mid \theta)$ Likelihood How well $\theta$ explains data
$P(\theta)$ Prior Our belief before seeing data
$P(D)$ Evidence Normalizing constant

Bayesian inference is “inverting” the generative process: given observed effects, infer the most likely causes.

Random Variables and Expectation

A random variable $X$ is a measurable function $X: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$. Its expectation:

\[\mathbb{E}[X] = \int x \, dP(x) = \begin{cases} \sum_x x \, p(x) & \text{(discrete)} \\ \int x \, f(x) \, dx & \text{(continuous)} \end{cases}\]

Key properties: linearity ($\mathbb{E}[aX + bY] = a\mathbb{E}[X] + b\mathbb{E}[Y]$), and for independent $X, Y$: $\mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y]$.

Variance and Covariance

\[\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])^2] = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2\] \[\text{Cov}(X, Y) = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mu_X)(Y - \mu_Y)]\]

The covariance matrix $\Sigma$ of a random vector $\mathbf{x}$: $\Sigma_{ij} = \text{Cov}(x_i, x_j)$. It is always positive semi-definite.

Law of Large Numbers & Central Limit Theorem

  • LLN: $\bar{X}_n \xrightarrow{P} \mu$ as $n \to \infty$ — sample means converge to the true mean
  • CLT: $\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n - \mu) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ — the distribution of sample means is approximately Gaussian

These justify why SGD works: averaging over mini-batches gives unbiased gradient estimates that converge.

Reference

C. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning. Springer, 2006, Ch. 1–2.
entry.summary: Probability theory is the framework for reasoning under uncertainty, covering probability spaces, Bayes' rule, random variables, and the central limit theorem.

entry.title: 4. Common Distributions
entry.content:
Knowing the right distribution family is half the modeling battle. Here we catalog the distributions that appear most frequently in ML.

Discrete Distributions

Bernoulli: a single binary trial with success probability $p$.

\[p(x) = p^x (1-p)^{1-x}, \quad x \in \{0, 1\}\]

Categorical: generalization to $K$ classes with probabilities $\boldsymbol{\pi}$.

\[p(x = k) = \pi_k, \quad \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k = 1\]

The output of a softmax layer defines a categorical distribution over classes.

Gaussian (Normal) Distribution

The most important distribution in ML:

\[\mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, \sigma^2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left( -\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} \right)\]

Multivariate Gaussian with mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and covariance $\Sigma$:

\[\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}, \Sigma) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2} |\Sigma|^{1/2}} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}) \right)\]

Why Gaussians are everywhere:

  • CLT: sums of many independent variables → Gaussian
  • Maximum entropy: among distributions with fixed mean and variance, Gaussian has the highest entropy
  • Conjugate prior: Gaussian likelihood × Gaussian prior = Gaussian posterior

Exponential Family

Many common distributions belong to the exponential family:

\[p(x \mid \boldsymbol{\eta}) = h(x) \exp\left( \boldsymbol{\eta}^\top \mathbf{T}(x) - A(\boldsymbol{\eta}) \right)\]

where $\boldsymbol{\eta}$ are natural parameters, $\mathbf{T}(x)$ are sufficient statistics, and $A(\boldsymbol{\eta})$ is the log-partition function.

Members include: Gaussian, Bernoulli, Categorical, Poisson, Gamma, Beta.

The log-partition function $A(\boldsymbol{\eta})$ is always convex, which guarantees that MLE has a unique solution.

Mixture Models

A Gaussian mixture model (GMM):

\[p(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k \, \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \Sigma_k)\]

GMMs are universal approximators of densities: with enough components, they can approximate any continuous distribution. They are trained via the EM algorithm.

Reference

K. Murphy, Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction. MIT Press, 2022, Ch. 2–3.
entry.summary: A catalog of the most frequently used distributions in ML, including Bernoulli, Gaussian, exponential family, and Gaussian mixture models.

entry.title: 5. Optimization Theory
entry.content:
Training a model = solving an optimization problem. Understanding the landscape of loss functions is essential for choosing the right algorithm.

Convexity

A function $f$ is convex if for all $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}$ and $\lambda \in [0,1]$:

\[f(\lambda \mathbf{x} + (1-\lambda) \mathbf{y}) \leq \lambda f(\mathbf{x}) + (1-\lambda) f(\mathbf{y})\]

Equivalently, $ abla^2 f(\mathbf{x}) \succeq 0$ everywhere. Convex problems have a crucial property: every local minimum is a global minimum.

Gradient Descent

The simplest first-order method:

\[\mathbf{x}_{t+1} = \mathbf{x}_t - \eta abla f(\mathbf{x}_t)\]

For an $L$-smooth, $\mu$-strongly convex function, GD with $\eta = 1/L$ converges at rate $O\left(\left( rac{L-\mu}{L+\mu} ight)^t ight)$.

Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)

When $f(\mathbf{x}) = rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f_i(\mathbf{x})$, computing the full gradient is expensive. SGD uses a mini-batch estimate:

\[\mathbf{x}_{t+1} = \mathbf{x}_t - \eta_t abla f_{B_t}(\mathbf{x}_t), \quad B_t \subset \{1, \dots, N\}\]
The stochastic gradient is an unbiased estimator: $\mathbb{E}[ abla f_{B_t}] = abla f$. The variance decreases as $O(1/ B_t )$.

Momentum and Adam

Momentum accumulates past gradients to dampen oscillations:

\[\mathbf{v}_{t+1} = eta \mathbf{v}_t + abla f(\mathbf{x}_t), \quad \mathbf{x}_{t+1} = \mathbf{x}_t - \eta \mathbf{v}_{t+1}\]

Adam combines momentum with adaptive per-parameter learning rates:

\[m_t = eta_1 m_{t-1} + (1- eta_1) g_t, \quad v_t = eta_2 v_{t-1} + (1- eta_2) g_t^2\] \[\mathbf{x}_{t+1} = \mathbf{x}_t - \eta rac{\hat{m}_t}{\sqrt{\hat{v}_t} + \epsilon}\]

where $\hat{m}_t, \hat{v}_t$ are bias-corrected estimates.

Constrained Optimization

For $\min f(\mathbf{x})$ subject to $g_i(\mathbf{x}) \leq 0$, the Lagrangian is:

\[\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, oldsymbol{\lambda}) = f(\mathbf{x}) + \sum_i \lambda_i g_i(\mathbf{x})\]

The KKT conditions (necessary for optimality):

  1. Stationarity: $ abla_\mathbf{x} \mathcal{L} = 0$
  2. Primal feasibility: $g_i(\mathbf{x}) \leq 0$
  3. Dual feasibility: $\lambda_i \geq 0$
  4. Complementary slackness: $\lambda_i g_i(\mathbf{x}) = 0$

This framework appears in SVM (dual formulation) and constrained RL (safe RL).

Reference

S. Boyd, L. Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization. Cambridge University Press, 2004.
entry.summary: Understanding the landscape of loss functions through convexity, gradient descent, SGD, momentum, Adam, and constrained optimization with KKT conditions.

entry.title: 6. Maximum Likelihood & MAP
entry.content:
How do we fit a model to data? The two most fundamental estimation principles are MLE and MAP.

Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)

Given data $D = {x_1, \dots, x_N}$ and a parametric model $p(x \mid \theta)$, MLE finds:

\[\theta_{\text{MLE}} = \arg\max_\theta \prod_{i=1}^N p(x_i \mid \theta) = \arg\max_\theta \sum_{i=1}^N \log p(x_i \mid \theta)\]

The log-likelihood $\ell(\theta) = \sum_i \log p(x_i \mid \theta)$ is easier to optimize. For exponential family distributions, $\ell(\theta)$ is concave, guaranteeing a global optimum.

Example — Gaussian MLE:

\[\mu_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N x_i, \quad \sigma^2_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i - \mu)^2\]

Note: the variance estimate is biased (divides by $N$, not $N-1$).

Maximum A Posteriori (MAP)

MAP adds a prior $p(\theta)$ via Bayes’ rule:

\[\theta_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_\theta \; p(\theta \mid D) = \arg\max_\theta \left[ \log p(D \mid \theta) + \log p(\theta) \right]\]

The prior acts as a regularizer:

  • Gaussian prior $p(\theta) \propto \exp(-\frac{\lambda}{2}|\theta|^2)$ → L2 regularization (Ridge)
  • Laplace prior $p(\theta) \propto \exp(-\lambda |\theta|_1)$ → L1 regularization (Lasso)

MLE vs MAP vs Full Bayesian

Approach Estimate Computation
MLE Point estimate $\hat{\theta}$ Optimize $\ell(\theta)$
MAP Point estimate with prior Optimize $\ell(\theta) + \log p(\theta)$
Full Bayesian Distribution $p(\theta \mid D)$ Integrate (often intractable)

As $N \to \infty$, MAP converges to MLE — the data overwhelms the prior.

Cross-Entropy Loss = Negative Log-Likelihood

In classification, the cross-entropy loss is exactly the negative log-likelihood of the categorical distribution:

\[\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^K y_{ik} \log \hat{p}_{ik}\]

This means training a classifier with cross-entropy loss is performing MLE.

Reference

C. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning. Springer, 2006, Ch. 1.2, 3.3.
entry.summary: The two most fundamental estimation principles — MLE and MAP — for fitting models to data, including their connection to regularization and cross-entropy loss.

entry.title: 7. Linear Models
entry.content:
Linear models are the simplest parametric models, yet they remain the building blocks of deep learning through their role as the final layers of neural networks.

Linear Regression

Model: $y = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b$. The ordinary least squares (OLS) solution minimizes:

\[\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{2N} \sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}_i)^2 = \frac{1}{2N} \|X\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{y}\|^2\]

Setting $\nabla_\mathbf{w} \mathcal{L} = 0$ gives the closed-form solution:

\[\mathbf{w}^* = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf{y}\]

This is also the MLE solution under the assumption $y \mid \mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}, \sigma^2)$.

Logistic Regression

For binary classification, we model $P(y=1 \mid \mathbf{x})$ using the sigmoid function:

\[\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}, \quad P(y=1 \mid \mathbf{x}) = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x})\]

The loss is the binary cross-entropy (negative log-likelihood of Bernoulli):

\[\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \left[ y_i \log \sigma(z_i) + (1-y_i) \log(1-\sigma(z_i)) \right]\]

This is a convex optimization problem — no local minima.

Softmax Regression

Generalization to $K$ classes. Define scores $z_k = \mathbf{w}_k^\top \mathbf{x}$ for each class, then:

\[P(y=k \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{\exp(z_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K \exp(z_j)} = \text{softmax}(\mathbf{z})_k\]

The softmax output is a valid probability distribution (non-negative, sums to 1).

Decision Boundaries

Linear models partition the input space with hyperplanes:

  • Binary: $\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b = 0$ defines the boundary
  • Multi-class: pairwise boundaries between class regions

The linearity limitation: cannot learn XOR or any non-linearly separable pattern without feature engineering. This motivates neural networks.

Reference

T. Hastie, R. Tibshirani, J. Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed. Springer, 2009, Ch. 3–4.
entry.summary: Linear models — including linear regression, logistic regression, and softmax regression — are the simplest parametric models and the building blocks of deep learning.

entry.title: 8. Bias-Variance Tradeoff
entry.content:
Generalization — performing well on unseen data — is the central challenge of ML. The bias-variance decomposition explains why.

The Decomposition

For a regression problem with true function $f(\mathbf{x})$ and noise $\epsilon$ (with $\mathbb{E}[\epsilon]=0$, $\text{Var}(\epsilon)=\sigma^2$), the expected prediction error of a model $\hat{f}$ is:

\[\mathbb{E}\left[(y - \hat{f}(\mathbf{x}))^2\right] = \underbrace{\left(f(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(\mathbf{x})]\right)^2}_{\text{Bias}^2} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\left[(\hat{f}(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(\mathbf{x})])^2\right]}_{\text{Variance}} + \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{Irreducible noise}}\]
  • Bias: error from wrong assumptions (model too simple)
  • Variance: error from sensitivity to training data (model too complex)
  • Noise: inherent randomness, cannot be reduced

Overfitting and Underfitting

Regime Bias Variance Symptom
Underfitting High Low Train error ↑, Test error ↑
Good fit Moderate Moderate Both errors reasonable
Overfitting Low High Train error ↓, Test error ↑

Regularization

Adding a penalty term to the loss to reduce variance:

L2 (Ridge): $\mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}} = \mathcal{L} + \lambda |\mathbf{w}|_2^2$

  • Shrinks all weights towards zero
  • Equivalent to Gaussian prior on $\mathbf{w}$

L1 (Lasso): $\mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}} = \mathcal{L} + \lambda |\mathbf{w}|_1$

  • Produces sparse solutions (some weights become exactly zero)
  • Equivalent to Laplace prior on $\mathbf{w}$
  • Useful for feature selection

Dropout (deep learning): randomly zero out neurons during training — an implicit ensemble method.

Cross-Validation

Estimate generalization error without a separate test set:

$k$-fold CV: split data into $k$ folds, train on $k-1$, validate on the held-out fold, repeat $k$ times, and average.

\[\text{CV}_k = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i=1}^k \mathcal{L}(\hat{f}^{(-i)}, D_i)\]

Common choices: $k=5$ or $k=10$. Leave-one-out ($k=N$) has low bias but high variance and is computationally expensive.

Reference

T. Hastie, R. Tibshirani, J. Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed. Springer, 2009, Ch. 7.
entry.summary: The bias-variance decomposition explains the central challenge of generalization, covering overfitting, underfitting, regularization, and cross-validation.

entry.title: 9. Kernel Methods & SVM
entry.content:
Kernel methods allow linear algorithms to learn non-linear decision boundaries by implicitly mapping data to high-dimensional feature spaces.

The Kernel Trick

Instead of explicitly computing a feature map $\phi(\mathbf{x})$, we define a kernel function:

\[k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \langle \phi(\mathbf{x}), \phi(\mathbf{x}') \rangle\]

Common kernels:

  • Linear: $k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}’) = \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{x}’$
  • Polynomial: $k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}’) = (\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{x}’ + c)^d$
  • RBF (Gaussian): $k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}’) = \exp\left(-\frac{|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}’|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)$

The RBF kernel maps to an infinite-dimensional feature space, yet the kernel evaluation is $O(d)$.

Mercer’s theorem: a function $k$ is a valid kernel if and only if the kernel matrix $K_{ij} = k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)$ is positive semi-definite for any set of inputs.

Support Vector Machine (SVM)

SVM finds the maximum-margin hyperplane separating two classes.

Primal problem (hard margin):

\[\min_{\mathbf{w}, b} \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 \quad \text{s.t.} \quad y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}_i + b) \geq 1, \; \forall i\]

The margin width is $\frac{2}{|\mathbf{w}|}$; maximizing margin = minimizing $|\mathbf{w}|$.

Dual problem (via Lagrange multipliers):

\[\max_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} \sum_i \alpha_i - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j} \alpha_i \alpha_j y_i y_j \mathbf{x}_i^\top \mathbf{x}_j \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \alpha_i \geq 0, \; \sum_i \alpha_i y_i = 0\]

Only data points with $\alpha_i > 0$ influence the decision boundary — these are the support vectors.

Soft Margin SVM

Real data is rarely linearly separable. The soft margin allows violations with slack variables $\xi_i$:

\[\min_{\mathbf{w}, b, \boldsymbol{\xi}} \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 + C\sum_i \xi_i \quad \text{s.t.} \quad y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}_i + b) \geq 1 - \xi_i, \; \xi_i \geq 0\]

$C$ controls the bias-variance tradeoff: large $C$ = low bias, high variance (tighter fit).

Kernel SVM

In the dual, data only appears via inner products $\mathbf{x}_i^\top \mathbf{x}_j$. Replacing with $k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)$ gives a non-linear SVM without changing the optimization structure.

Reference

B. Schölkopf, A. Smola, Learning with Kernels. MIT Press, 2002.
entry.summary: Kernel methods allow linear algorithms to learn non-linear decision boundaries by implicitly mapping data to high-dimensional feature spaces, with SVMs finding maximum-margin hyperplanes.

entry.title: 10. Probabilistic Graphical Models
entry.content:
Graphical models provide a language for expressing the structure of joint probability distributions — which variables depend on which.

Bayesian Networks

A Bayesian network (directed graphical model) represents a joint distribution as a product of conditionals:

\[p(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i \mid \text{Pa}(x_i))\]

where $\text{Pa}(x_i)$ are the parents of $x_i$ in the directed acyclic graph (DAG).

This factorization reduces the number of parameters from exponential to manageable. For example, a chain $x_1 \to x_2 \to x_3$ gives $p(x_1, x_2, x_3) = p(x_1) p(x_2 \mid x_1) p(x_3 \mid x_2)$.

Hidden Markov Models (HMMs)

An HMM is a temporal Bayesian network with:

  • Hidden states $z_t$ following a Markov chain: $p(z_t \mid z_{t-1})$
  • Observations $x_t$ emitted from hidden states: $p(x_t \mid z_t)$

Key inference tasks:

  • Filtering: $p(z_t \mid x_{1:t})$ — forward algorithm $O(TK^2)$
  • Smoothing: $p(z_t \mid x_{1:T})$ — forward-backward algorithm
  • Decoding: $\arg\max_{z_{1:T}} p(z_{1:T} \mid x_{1:T})$ — Viterbi algorithm

HMMs are foundational for speech recognition and biological sequence analysis.

The EM Algorithm

For models with latent variables $\mathbf{z}$, direct MLE over $\theta$ is intractable. The Expectation-Maximization algorithm iterates:

E-step: compute the posterior over latent variables

\[q(\mathbf{z}) = p(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{x}, \theta^{(t)})\]

M-step: maximize the expected complete-data log-likelihood

\[\theta^{(t+1)} = \arg\max_\theta \; \mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{z})} \left[ \log p(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z} \mid \theta) \right]\]

EM monotonically increases the marginal likelihood $p(\mathbf{x} \mid \theta)$ and converges to a local optimum. It is used to train GMMs, HMMs, and other latent variable models.

Variational Inference (Preview)

When the E-step is intractable (complex posteriors), variational inference approximates $p(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{x})$ with a simpler distribution $q(\mathbf{z})$ by minimizing:

\[\text{KL}(q(\mathbf{z}) \| p(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{x})) = -\text{ELBO} + \log p(\mathbf{x})\]

Maximizing the ELBO (Evidence Lower Bound) is equivalent to minimizing the KL divergence. This idea leads directly to the VAE (see Post 15).

Reference

D. Koller, N. Friedman, Probabilistic Graphical Models. MIT Press, 2009.
entry.summary: Graphical models provide a language for expressing the structure of joint probability distributions, covering Bayesian networks, HMMs, EM, and variational inference.
